script: as stored in the canonical MorphoVerse dataset for this poem (Perso-Arabic or Devanagari; verify per-record rather than assuming)
romanization_guidance: Kashmiri is written in both Perso-Arabic (Nastaliq-based) and Devanagari scripts depending on source and community; identify which script the specific poem's original_poem text actually uses before romanizing, rather than assuming one.

Kashmiri vowel representation is genuinely uncertain across both scripts for a non-specialist reader; when a term's vowel quality cannot be confidently determined from the written form alone, choose the most common reader-friendly rendering and flag the uncertainty via translation_note rather than presenting one romanization as definitively correct.
Use a widely-recognized conventional spelling for well-known names/places when one already exists in common English usage.
Keep every repeated occurrence of the same source term romanized identically within one poem.
linguistic_guidance: Kashmiri (Koshur) is a distinct Dardic language, not a dialect of Urdu, Hindi, or Persian, even though it may be written in a Perso-Arabic script and shares vocabulary with those languages -- do not conflate Kashmiri with Urdu/Hindi/Persian identity when identifying cultural or linguistic content.

Because Kashmiri is comparatively under-resourced in existing NLP/annotation tooling, prefer maximally specific, text-grounded loss_note and translation_note content over a generic gloss whenever a genuine loss is identified -- do not compensate for uncertainty by writing a vaguer note.
Vocabulary shared with Persian, Urdu, or Sanskrit registers is not automatically Kashmiri-specific -- assess each term's actual role in this poem's own text.
cultural_boundary_rules: A culturally specific Kashmiri annotation requires a defensible link to a named tradition, practice, or symbol that the poem's own text actually evidences -- do not add one merely because the poem is in Kashmiri.

Do not infer Kashmiri Sufi tradition, Shaivite (Kashmir Shaivism) tradition, chinar trees, snow landscapes, pheran clothing, the samovar, shrine imagery, or conflict/political imagery unless the poem's own words name or unambiguously depict that specific content -- these are common outside shorthands for 'Kashmiri culture' (including in ways that risk politicizing or exoticizing the poem) and must not be assumed as a default backdrop.

Words for tavern, wine, garden, moon, longing, loneliness, and general spiritual vocabulary are not automatically Kashmiri-specific cultural cues -- this vocabulary is shared across Persianate and Sufi poetic traditions broadly; treat it as culturally specific only when the poem's own text gives it a specific, named, or clearly bounded Kashmiri role.

Distinguish Kashmiri-specific culture from the broader Persianate, Sanskritic, Sufi, and Shaivite traditions it shares vocabulary and imagery with -- shared vocabulary is not proof of Kashmiri-specific content, and Kashmiri-specific content should not be flattened into a generic 'Persianate/Sufi' label either.
literary_context_cautions: Kashmiri literary history includes distinct major voices and traditions (Lal Ded's mystic vakhs, Sufi Rishi-order verse, Habba Khatoon-style romantic lyric, modern lyric poetry) -- do not assume a poem belongs to a specific one without textual evidence, and do not force a single tradition onto a poem consistent with more than one.
Do not assume every Kashmiri poem engages with political conflict or displacement; annotate only what the poem's own text supports.
translation_cautions: Watch for script-transition ambiguity itself producing a translation/transliteration side-effect (a term rendered differently depending on which script the source used) -- document this explicitly rather than silently normalizing it.
Because of Kashmiri's under-resourced status, prefer a specific, well-evidenced loss_note over a shorter, vaguer one whenever a genuine translation loss is identified.
figurative_language_cautions: Mystic/Sufi-register vocabulary (longing, wine, the beloved, union) may be genuinely ambiguous between secular-romantic and devotional-mystic readings; do not resolve this ambiguity by default assumption -- use the text's own evidence, and use the explicit-uncertainty mechanism when it is genuinely unresolvable.
visual_representation_cautions: When a cultural or figurative element is genuinely visualizable, offer multiple acceptable_visual_variants rather than a single fixed scene, and do not default to chinar-tree, snow-landscape, or shrine imagery unless the text specifically supports it.

negative_confusions for a Kashmiri entity should name a plausible, specific incorrect substitution, not a generic stereotype, and should not default to politically-charged imagery absent direct textual evidence.
stereotype_avoidance_rules: Do not adopt a 'you are steeped in an ancient, endangered, irreplaceable tradition' framing when annotating -- this kind of framing pressures romanticized or overconfident cultural claims; annotate only what this specific poem's text supports.

Do not apply a numeric quota (e.g. 'expect N cultural entities') to this poem -- the pilot's own sanity-check use case demonstrates a Kashmiri poem can have zero cultural entities and that is a valid outcome, not an incomplete annotation.
ambiguity_handling_rules: When a term's script origin, vowel quality, or Sufi-versus-secular reading is genuinely uncertain, prefer the more conservative reading and use the explicit-uncertainty mechanism rather than asserting a specific interpretation as fact.
Preserve genuine polysemy in Kashmiri mystic vocabulary rather than collapsing it to a single English sense.
prohibited_assumptions: Do not assume the speaker's religion (Kashmiri poetry spans Hindu Pandit, Muslim, and secular voices) beyond what the text states.
Do not assume a specific historical or political period unless the text itself places the poem there.
Do not assume which script the underlying dataset record uses without checking the actual original_poem text.
Do not assume gender beyond what the text states.
